extracted.intended_audience: journal editors, publishers, research administrators, funders, and researchers interested in peer-review reform
extracted.subtask_description: An opinion article arguing for remunerating peer reviewers and regulating submission volumes; surveys existing and proposed peer-review models, practical implementation options (who pays, how much), safeguards against corruption, and systemic reforms to the academic ecosystem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Referees' impartiality and competency
rubrics_metrics.description: Peer review relies on the elusive concepts of referees’ impartiality and competency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Maintain reviewer impartiality and competence as core standards; recognise that process limitations (bias, inconsistency, slow turnaround) often stem from failures to secure impartial, competent reviewers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying reviewers (monetary compensation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Monetarily compensating peer reviewers fairly and transparently is proposed as a viable solution to increase reviewer availability and motivation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Suggested remuneration examples: ~$200 per review (general) or $450 for for-profit publishers; payment should be fair, transparent, and accompanied by safeguards to avoid corruption and low-quality rapid reviews.

rubrics_metrics.name: Professional reviewers as a career
rubrics_metrics.description: Create part-time or full-time professional reviewers (managed by universities or for‑profit companies) who can be paid to review a set number of papers (e.g., 2–3 papers/week).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Professional reviewers could attract retired senior researchers and others who enjoy reviewing; professional role should be regulated by ethical/professional standards and integrated with editorial workflows similar to paid language editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulate number of submissions per author
rubrics_metrics.description: Persuade researchers or implement rules to limit submissions to their most novel and useful research (e.g., cap how many papers an author can submit per year).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Capping submissions aims to bring volumes to manageable levels and reduce strain on peer review; would require rethinking citation-based productivity metrics and institutional incentives.

rubrics_metrics.name: Submission fee to fund reviewer payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Levy a submission fee (proposed example: $200) charged for submissions sent for review; submission fees can be deducted from APCs if the paper is accepted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Submission fees can finance paid reviewers and discourage low-quality mass submissions; should be charged only for manuscripts sent for external review and transparently managed to avoid increasing APC burden unnecessarily.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reviewers as consultants (grant-budgeted fees)
rubrics_metrics.description: Treat peer reviewers as consultants whose contributions can be budgeted in grants as consultancy/publication-related fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This approach integrates reviewer payment into existing grant budgets but may increase financial pressure on funding bodies and requires clear guidance from funders about allowable costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hybrid two-tier system (prepublication for high-impact work only)
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement a two-tier model where only submissions judged likely to have significant impact are sent for prepublication peer review; other papers are published with post-publication review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces pressure on reviewers but risks bias toward top labs and raises questions about objective initial impact assessment and how unreviewed papers count in metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Non-selective review model (methodological soundness focus)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask reviewers to evaluate only methodological soundness (e.g., methods and results) rather than novelty, impact, or predicted citations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Speeds review and reduces demand on reviewers' judgement about importance; can be paired with post-publication evaluation of significance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Open, continuous, interactive peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Transform peer review into an open, continuous, interactive forum where authors, reviewers, and editors interact in real time to promote engagement rather than judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facilitates transparent discussion and diverse stakeholder input; relies on platforms that enable sustained conversations and moderation to avoid harassment or noise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Independent peer review platforms / paid pre-submission services
rubrics_metrics.description: Use independent review services (e.g., Rubriq, Editage) where authors pay reviewers to improve manuscripts before journal submission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Can improve manuscript quality before journal review but adds cost to authors and may advantage better-funded researchers; possible complement to journal-based review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portable peer review across journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt journal-independent peer review (portable reviews) so reviews and revisions can travel with manuscripts across participating journals (e.g., Review Commons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reduces duplicate reviewing across journals and makes reviewer effort reusable; may add delays while finding a suitable journal but can improve efficiency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Merge journals into mega-journals with large editorial boards
rubrics_metrics.description: Use mega-journal models (broad scope, large editorial boards) to handle very large submission volumes with relatively efficient turnaround.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large reviewer pools and lower selectivity can speed processing, but specialized domains may still require focused journals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build an online reviewer registry accessible by journals
rubrics_metrics.description: Create a large collaborative registry of volunteer reviewers that journals can query to identify potential referees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Registry should be maintained by cross-publisher partnerships, include diverse expertise and demographics, and be resourced for sustainability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Augment peer review with technology
rubrics_metrics.description: Use technology (automated checks, AI, software platforms) to detect statistical flaws, figure manipulation, and streamline workflows.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Automated tools can flag issues and reduce reviewer burden; adoption of generative AI will have profound effects and must be handled carefully to avoid false flags and gaming.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reciprocity model: review proportional to publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Require that researchers who publish more should contribute more to peer review (‘you review as much as you publish’).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aims for fairness in workload distribution, but may be infeasible for senior authors with other duties and does not account for review quality or time availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Offer incentives and rewards (non-monetary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Provide non-monetary rewards such as certificates, discounts, free access to publisher products, vouchers, conference fee reductions, recognition in reviewer databases, and editorial appointments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These incentives can increase participation but have so far not stemmed reviewer decline; combine with other measures for greater effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Link peer review involvement to academic benefits
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognize peer-review activity in promotion, continuing-education credits, waived publication fees, or (in rare cases) co-authorship when reviewers materially improve manuscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional recognition could boost intrinsic motivation; must avoid perverse incentives (e.g., co-authorship for minor suggestions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-publication peer review (PPPR)
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt post-publication peer review models where all submissions are published and reviewed openly after publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PPPR supports continuous improvement and openness but needs safeguards to prevent low-quality material flooding public record; may require limits on how long papers remain open for formal discussion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustainability and funding considerations for paid reviews
rubrics_metrics.description: Assess who will pay for reviewer remuneration (publishers, submission fees, funders, institutions) and whether paying reviewers is sustainable given journal volume and domain differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment models must consider publisher profit motives (for-profit publishers may resist), multidisciplinary journals' high costs, and equity across domains; multiple funding sources may be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Safeguards against unethical practices when paying reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Implement protections (editor evaluation/rating of reviews prior to payment, disclosure of paid review tasks, conflict-of-interest checks, limits on reviewing outside expertise) to prevent corruption and low-quality paid reviews.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Editors should approve and rate completed reviews before payment; publishers must adopt ethical/professional standards and auditing to counter fabricated reports and paper-mill behaviour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paying reviewers in context of economic disparity
rubrics_metrics.description: Be mindful that per-review payments may disproportionately attract reviewers from low- and middle-income countries and could create over-involvement or inequities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Mitigations include capping invitations to reviewers from low-income countries relative to readership or author representation, and full public declaration of paid review tasks to allow editorial oversight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guard against proliferation of for-profit peer-review agencies and paper mills
rubrics_metrics.description: Recognise the risk that paying reviewers could spawn for-profit agencies with dubious practices (fabricated reports, low-quality reviews).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Require accreditation, transparent practices, editorial oversight, and community standards to ensure agencies meet ethical norms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinants for reviewer remuneration
rubrics_metrics.description: Determine pay according to multiple factors: for-profit vs not-for-profit journals, scientific domain funding level, number of reviewers required, article type, length and complexity, average reviewer hours, and average yearly number of manuscripts reviewed per reviewer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishers/editors should estimate remuneration based on typical hours per article type and community norms; professional bodies (COPE, DORA, EASE) could provide general guidelines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of paid review tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Publishers should publicly declare reviewers' paid review tasks so editors and the community can see reviewers' levels of involvement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency enables detection of unusual review dynamics and helps manage conflicts of interest and reviewer workload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editor involvement in selection, training, and diversity of reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Editors should play a more efficient role in selecting prospective reviewers, improving reviewer diversity, and facilitating reviewer training.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Better editorial selection, training programs, and attention to diversity can improve review quality and reviewer availability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluation of review quality tied to payment
rubrics_metrics.description: Tie reviewer remuneration or continued eligibility for paid reviews to editorial evaluation/ratings of review quality and thoroughness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payment should be contingent on satisfactory review quality to avoid quick superficial reviews motivated solely by payment; editorial oversight required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise potential negative impacts of paying reviewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Be aware that monetary rewards may decrease review quality, reduce intrinsic motivation, create multi-tier systems favouring wealthier journals, and increase APCs or subscription fees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design payment schemes and complementary non-monetary incentives carefully, monitor quality outcomes, and seek equity-minded policies to prevent unintended harms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alternative compensation models (institutional or group payments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Instead of paying individual reviewers, consider compensating reviewers' institutions or labs, or awarding group prizes whose proceeds support research or underrepresented members.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Could reduce individual over-incentivisation but may ignore that much review work happens off-hours; requires clear rules on allocation and transparency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Systemic reform to address publish-or-perish
rubrics_metrics.description: Address root causes — the 'publish or perish' culture — by promoting dissemination schemes that value quality over quantity and collaboration over competition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reforms could include changing promotion metrics, capping submissions, encouraging preprints for less-critical work, and universities owning dissemination to reduce reliance on for-profit publishers.
